partial_case.facts: The resident moved into his property on 2 January 2024. He said that the landlord was aware he had multiple health conditions such as aquagenic pruritus, sickle cell trait, chronic pain, depression and anxiety. However, the landlord said it had no recorded vulnerabilities for the resident. The resident reported multiples repairs since February 2024. Although the landlord carried out repairs, the resident said some repairs remained outstanding. On 23 April 2024, the resident raised a complaint about the landlord's handling of the repairs since he moved in. He explained that although the landlord had scheduled a date for the kitchen and bedroom window repairs, it had not addressed the living room and bathroom windows. He described significant gaps above the kitchen kickboards, where debris and dirt had gathered. He said that the landlord had failed to adequately clean the property. He was dissatisfied the landlord had informed him it could not replace his kitchen cabinets for another 10 years and this contradicted its lettable standard. He added that the energy report provided at the start of tenancy highlighted deficiencies that concerned him. As a resolution he sought compensation, replacement of the kitchen cabinets and thorough cleaning of the kitchen, reimbursement for the floor planks he purchased to rectify uneven floors, and prompt resolution of all outstanding repairs.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord failed to maintain accurate and complete repair records, which undermined its ability to monitor progress, reschedule appointments, and confirm that it had resolved the issues. In addition, there were significant delays in completing repairs and it did not consistently and effectively communicate with the resident on the works. It also failed to consider the resident's vulnerabilities and review its handling of the repairs against its repairs policy.

The landlord responded twice at stage 1, which is not in line with the Housing Ombudsman's Complaint Handling Code (the Code). This delayed the complaint process and caused confusion as to the escalation and fair process.

partial_case.facts: The resident moved into the property on 2 January 2024 and said the landlord was aware of multiple health conditions; the landlord said it had no recorded vulnerabilities. The resident reported multiple repairs from February 2024, and said some repairs remained outstanding after the landlord carried out some works. The complaint concerned the landlord’s handling of repairs in the property and the associated complaint. On 23 April 2024, the resident complained about the landlord’s handling of repairs since he moved in and sought compensation, replacement kitchen cabinets, cleaning, reimbursement for flooring, and prompt resolution of outstanding repairs. On 24 September 2024, the resident complained that several repairs remained unresolved, including heating, wall, window, worktop, gaps, protruding nails, step, insulation and soundproofing issues, and he sought a rent refund, compensation, and reimbursement for flooring. The landlord issued a second stage 1 response on 23 October 2024 and a stage 2 complaint response on 15 November 2024. The resident referred the matter to the Ombudsman in November 2024 and sought completion of outstanding repairs, compensation, a rent refund from January 2024, prioritisation for major works, and improvements to complaint handling. On 14 January 2025, the landlord offered £210 compensation to the resident.

orders: Pay £650 compensation to the resident, inclusive of the landlord’s £210 offer if already paid
Discuss the resident’s vulnerabilities and disabilities and update records
Review why repairs and complaint handling policies/procedures were not followed

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord failed to maintain accurate and complete repair records, which undermined its ability to monitor progress, reschedule appointments, and confirm that it had resolved the issues.
In addition, there were significant delays in completing repairs and it did not consistently and effectively communicate with the resident on the works.
It also failed to consider the resident’s vulnerabilities and review its handling of the repairs against its repairs policy.
The landlord responded twice at stage 1, which is not in line with the Housing Ombudsman’s Complaint Handling Code (the Code).
The landlord should have considered its obligations under the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998.
The landlord failed to keep accurate and up to date records of the repairs.
